Q: Is Java still worth learning to get a job soon? Seniors — please spit the truth A:

I have been hearing trolls (including some co-workers) say “Java is dying” for 20 years. It is still quite strong with no signs of decline. It is also a pleasure to work with, thanks to its superb documentation. Much as I hate Spring, it is a dominant framework right now, so learning it will probably increase your chances of being hired.

Q: How to invoke NTP sync from python on windows? A:

This is how to use 'w32tm /resync' without any changes in windows settings or behaviour:

import ctypes, time
resync = ctypes.windll.shell32.ShellExecuteW(
    None,
    u"runas",
    u"cmd.exe",
    u'/c net start w32time && w32tm /resync && net stop w32time',
    # /k : leave cmd window open, /c : close cmd window after execution
    None,
    2 # 1 normal window, 2 minimized, 3 maximized
    )

time.sleep(5)

As default, the w32time service in windows, is stopped (see AididDev answer). The ntp sync is made by a specific task from the task scheduler.

Check the service state to be stopped, otherwise the command sequence won't be executed.

To make the sync from python, on our demand, we need to start the service, make the sync, then stop the service, as admin (Run batch files with admin rights via Python as example) . Using ctypes we link the commands with '&&' making them to execute in succession. Time.sleep(x) is necessary in order to keep the cmd window open until all the commands are executed.

Using option '2' and '/c' the command window will be minimized and will close after execution.

Use it as function, triggered by your condition, in the main code or in a new thread if time spent is important.

Q: Extract the selected text in custom iOS keyboard extension A:

In a custom keyboard extension you cannot reliably obtain the full selected text. The system restricts access to small context windows via UITextDocumentProxy.

To work around this, use

  • clipboard-based workflows
  • host app integration
  • explicit user paste actions

Q: error: ‘format’ attribute argument 3 value ‘7’ does not refer to a variable argument list A:

I posted it in GCC Bugzilla. The short answer is:

format does not work with variable templates type. It only works with variable argument list.

The documentation should make this clear.

I found for me this "suitable" solution:

  1. In the main include file I added #define CHECK_PRINT_PARAMETERS false|true
  2. In the include file where I define the FAEWE_LOG* templates/functions I have #if CHECK_PRINT_PARAMETERS == false
  3. In this case the existing template definition is processed - without the printf parameter check.
  4. #if CHECK_PRINT_PARAMETERS == true "opens" for gcc a totally different code, where I only declare all of the log functions - as dummy. In my case I had to write this code:
__attribute__((format(printf, 1, 2)))
auto FAEWE_LOG_SERVER( const char *, ... ) -> void;

__attribute__((format(printf, 2, 3)))
auto FAEWE_LOG_SERVER( const LogControllerMode, const char *, ... ) -> void;

__attribute__((format(printf, 1, 2)))
auto FAEWE_LOG_THREAD( const char *, ... ) -> void;

__attribute__((format(printf, 2, 3)))
auto FAEWE_LOG_THREAD( const char, const char *, ... ) -> void;

__attribute__((format(printf, 2, 3)))
auto FAEWE_LOG_THREAD( const LogControllerMode, const char *, ... ) -> void;

__attribute__((format(printf, 4, 5)))
auto FAEWE_LOG( const uint, const LogControllerMode, const std::vector<LogControllerType> &,
                const char *, ... ) -> void;

__attribute__((format(printf, 2, 3)))
auto FAEWE_LOG( const uint , const char *, ... ) -> void;

template<class BaseClass>  // Extends each class with the log functionality
class LoggingClass
{

};

With this, I didn't have to touch/change one of the hundreds FAEWE_LOG* function and everything works like before.

Because these are only declaration, linking fails - and this is in my case the "desired" behaviour, because then the dummy functions never generate an executable.

This works "perfectly", and when I ran it the first time, gcc pointed out half dozens of not 100% correct format specifiers. Yes, I have to run the check manually, but this is better than having somewhere a bug. I am a human who makes mistakes/errors/bugs.

In my eyes, C++ "degenerated" with the std::cout and similar functions printf. Somehow, as they wanted to "force" the beauty of "argument piping" but I have the feeling, no one of the guys ever wrote a logging function with lot of different parameters formatted for a human. As long there is no a similar C++ function, I stick with printf.

Already curious what the reason for closing of this question is... But I could answer it before it got closed.

Q: How to fix floating point error in R for the root of a covariance matrix? A:

One option to fix the problem is to rescale the numbers.

Floating point errors are caused by values that are close to zero. If the values are transformed to be away from zero, there will be fewer floating point errors.
